Practice calls for coordination between the hands: first fix the touch point and the pluck, then add the bending of the rod and the vibrato.

With a pickup added it enters ensembles and contemporary Asian pop and rock, and guitar electronics can be used with it to extend its sound. It is also common in Vietnamese traditional orchestras; Vietnamese musicians have arranged several concertos for it, so that the đàn bầu takes part in concerto performance as a solo instrument.

Some five hundred years ago the Jing people who moved from Haiphong to Fangchenggang brought the instrument into China. It was made of bamboo at first and of other materials later. Because its volume is small, it was long confined to solo playing, folk music and the accompaniment of poetry recitation, and blind musicians were often its players. After the invention of the magnetic pickup the đàn bầu entered ensembles, contemporary Asian pop and rock, and Vietnamese traditional orchestras; Vietnamese musicians have also arranged several concertos in which it is played.

The right hand plucks with a long plectrum and the little finger touches the seven common nodes lightly, giving the first seven harmonics; the left hand bends a soft rod to raise or lower the pitch and to add vibrato. Its acoustic volume is on the small side, and the magnetic pickup and guitar electronics extend where it can be used. It is basically the same instrument as the duxianqin of the Jing in China; acoustically it is almost identical in form to the Đàn Máng of the Mường, with little difference in timbre.

The đàn bầu is a Vietnamese single-string zither, classified for sound production under 314/315/316 zithers / struck / keyed chordophones. It was once built of a bamboo tube, a wooden rod, a coconut shell and silk strings; today it usually has a wooden resonator, electric-guitar strings and a tuner, and the gourd is often only decoration. The player touches the harmonic points lightly with the little finger of the right hand, plucks the string with a plectrum held between thumb and index finger, and moves a flexible rod with the left hand to change the pitch or add vibrato. Historically it was often played by blind musicians, for solo playing and to accompany poetry, and it also appears in Vietnamese traditional orchestras; the Jing call it the duxianqin.
早期彈匏為竹製管形齊特琴，由竹管、木桿、半個椰子殼與絲弦組成；竹管為琴身，木桿垂: The early đàn bầu was a bamboo tube zither made of a bamboo tube, a wooden rod, half a coconut shell and a silk string; the bamboo tube was the body, the wooden rod was fixed upright, the coconut shell served as the resonator and the silk string was the sounding body. Modern instruments replace the bamboo tube with a wooden soundboard, with hardwood for the sides and softwood in the middle, and use electric-guitar strings; the gourd is usually made of wood now and serves mainly as decoration, and a modern tuning device is fitted. The materials of the other parts are not recorded in the source.
